title: Solution epitaxy of single-crystal ferroelectric p-i-n structure with ultrahigh photovoltaic response

paper_content.abstract: Ferroelectric materials with a switchable polarization are appealing for optoelectronic applications because of their above-bandgap photovoltage with a potential to exceed the Shockley-Queisser limit efficiency within classic p-n junctions. However, the intrinsic photovoltaic current in ferroelectrics remains far below the junction ones by orders, hindering their practical applications. Here we report an extremely large photovoltaic current density of 130 mA cm-2 with a photovoltage of 1.31 V under 375 nm light illumination in single-domain lead titanate films. Its photoresponsivity surpasses all available ferroelectric materials by two orders of magnitude. Systematic investigations reveal that an interfacial Ta dopant layer during solution epitaxy drives a polarization converting of the film via the flexoelectric effect, where surface charged Pb vacancy layer was generated for polarization screening. These two layers produce a p-i-n structure throughout the film, accounting for the ultrahigh photovoltaic response. Furthermore, a self-powered X-ray detector made of such film was explored to achieve a sensitivity of 4.73 C Gy –1 air cm–3, three orders of magnitude higher than that of commercial amorphous Se detectors. Our findings may pave the way for exploring novel detection and imaging devices based on ferroelectric materials.
paper_content.introduction:
The photovoltaic (PV) effect in semiconductors is the foundation of many technologies, such as solar energy conversion1, photocatalysis2 and optoelectronic sensing3. The key step to these applications is efficiently driving charge separation of electron-hole pair carriers or excitons by a built-in electric field and subsequent carrier transport. Towards this purpose, classic p-n junction was fabricated in the crystalline silicon solar cells. Nevertheless, the efficiency of solar-cell is curtailed by inherent energy losses, subjected to the Shockley-Queisser (S-Q) limit in single p-n junction4,5. Alternatively, perovskite oxide ferroelectric semiconductors, have triggered great interests for solar energy conversion6–8, where the above-bandgap voltage from several to several thousand volts can even be produced in single-phase ferroelectrics such as LiNbO 9, holding a potential to exceed such efficiency limit5. Interestingly, an electric polarization-direction-dependent PV effect has been demonstrated in BiFeO 3 (BFO)10. However, the resulting PV current density turns out to be quite low mainly due to poor bulk conductivity. Different strategies ranging from the enhanced absorption by doping11, high-efficient carrier collection by atomic force microscope (AFM) tips12,13 and polar order engineering14 have been developed to improve the PV current. Despite great efforts towards polarization-based PV effect in the past decades, the intrinsic PV current in ferroelectrics is still at the level of μA cm-2. The PV current mechanisms in ferroelectrics are still complex and controversial, involving shift current, ballistic current, and incompletely screened depolarization field or domain walls15. Despite of great efforts, an effective strategy to significantly improve PV current in ferroelectrics towards practical devices remain a big challenge16.

For typical crystalline silicon or halide perovskite solar cells, the p-n junction or p-i-n structure plays a decisive role in achieving efficient energy conversion17,18, where electron and hole transport layers as well as built-in electric field design are achieved simultaneously. For example, in halide perovskite solar cells, meticulous selection of transport layers and precise band structure matching are essential for optimizing p-i-n functionality. Nevertheless, analogous transport layers and their derived built-in electric field throughout single-phase ferroelectrics have not been explored yet. But it is very encouraging that intriguing electrical conductivity phenomena near domain walls have been discovered19 and illustrated systematically20. N-type or p-type conducting layer near domain walls in ferroelectrics could be generated through spatial confinement of charged defects, such as Bi vacancies and oxygen vacancies, compensating bound charges due to a spontaneous polarization discontinuity21. Interestingly, p-n junction based on single domain wall have been designed experimentally22. These advances suggest a possibility to enhance the PV current through domain wall confining charged defects. However, non-uniform direction of built-in electric field near every domain wall is not beneficial for unidirectional photogenerated carrier separation and transport. Moreover, domain walls have been identified to contribute to the high photovoltage rather than the PV current23.

In addition to domain walls, the polarization surface of single-domain ferroelectrics have been demonstrated to energetically confine various charged point defects for screening bound charges24. In principle, these defect layers near the opposite polarization surface can serve as electron and hole transport layers, as well as constructing a p-i-n structure to enhance the PV effect. Especially, it has been proved that oxygen vacancy layer is prevailed as a screening manner near the negative polarization surface of ferroelectrics25–27. However, oxygen vacancies hardly contribute to n-type conduction in perovskite ferroelectric oxides because of forming polarons by trapping electrons28,29.

In this work, we developed a strategy to control the polarization direction of single-domain ferroelectric lead titanate (PbTiO , PTO) films by an interfacial Ta dopant during a solution epitaxy. This enables constructing a p-i-n structure throughout the films, where the interfacial Ta doping layer and the polarization screening induced surface Pb vacancy layer can be employed as efficient n-type electron and p-type hole transport layers, respectively. As a result, an ultrahigh PV current density of 130 mA cm-2 with a photovoltage of 1.31 V under 375 nm light illumination was obtained, two orders of magnitude higher than that of emerging ferroelectric materials. Using these films, a self-powered and direct-type X-ray detector was fabricated to demonstrate high sensitivity and stability which is highly desired for next generation X-ray imaging devices.
paper_content.results:
Single-crystal single-domain pure PTO and Ta doped PTO (Ta-PTO) films have been grown with a solution epitaxy method30 on single-crystal 0.7% Nb doped SrTiO (NSTO) substrates at a relatively low temperature (~200°C) (see methods for more details). X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed that both films exhibit a tetragonal perovskite structure (JCPDS#70-0746) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). As shown in Supplementary Fig. 1b, a single Ta-PTO (103) diffraction peak is observed together with the NSTO (103) substrate peak, indicating epitaxial growth of the Ta-PTO film on the NSTO substrate. Additionally, 𝜙 scan revealed four peaks at 90° intervals, indicating the single-crystal nature of the Ta-PTO film (Supplementary Fig. 1c), which also has a smooth and continuous surface (Supplementary Fig. 1d). For tetragonal perovskite PTO, the spontaneous polarization (P ) arises from the off-center displacements of Ti ions31, was analyzed using atomic-resolution high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Fig. 3). As shown in Fig. 1a, Ti ions in the pure PTO film display upward displacements relative to the Pb ion columns, indicating a downward polarization along the film's thickness direction. The thickness of the pure PTO film is ~1030 nm. In contrast, Fig. 1b reveals opposite displacements of Ti ions in the Ta-PTO film, with a thickness of ~1100 nm. The out-of-plane displacement of Ti ions in Ta-PTO increases to ~0.20 Å at the surface, slightly smaller than the ~0.26 Å observed for pure PTO. Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) confirms that the Ta-PTO film exhibits typical ferroelectric characteristics with a single-domain configuration (Supplementary Fig. 4). Furthermore, the rocking curves scanned around the (002) diffraction peak further confirms the single-crystal nature of the films (Supplementary Fig. 5), with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 0.385° for Ta-PTO and 0.237° for pure PTO, further supporting the single-domain configuration.

To uncover the mechanism behind the opposite polarization direction in pure PTO and Ta-PTO films, we analyzed their interface structures. Fig. 1c,d show the lattice parameters a and c. The interfacial c-value in Ta-PTO (~3.99 Å) is smaller than in pure PTO (~4.11 Å). Notably, it increases to ~4.15 Å within the first three unit cells above the interface, indicating an inhomogeneous compressive strain (~3.86%) between the interface and the inner regions of the Ta-PTO film. The interfacial strain was further analyzed using geometric phase analysis (GPA) based on atomic-level HAADF-STEM images (Supplementary Fig. 6). As shown in Fig. 1e,f, unlike pure PTO film, Ta-PTO film exhibits a distinct interfacial compressive strain (ε ) layer, likely caused by the incorporation of Ta dopants, considering the slightly larger ionic radius of Ta5+ (0.640 Å) compared to Ti4+ (0.605 Å)32. At the nanoscale, a large stress gradient can induce a local electric field via the flexoelectric effect. Such gradients can be generated artificially, for example by localized mechanical loading with an AFM tip, as widely reported to induce flexoelectric fields and control ferroelectric polarization33,34. This effect arises from the coupling between a strain gradient and ferroelectric polarization35. Moreover, phase-field modeling was used to calculate the flexoelectric field within the PTO layer caused by strain gradient from local concentration inhomogeneity36 (Supplementary Note 1). As shown in Fig. 1g, the calculated field strength at six unit cells can be up to 130 kV cm-1, much higher than the coercive field (E ) of PTO37, enabling polarization reversal. This flexoelectric effect energetically favors the reversal of the polarization direction of the Ta-PTO film layer near the interface from downward to upward, creating a built-in field that could switch the polarization throughout the film (Fig. 1h).

The opposite polarization direction of the films shown in Fig. 1a,b necessitate different screening mechanisms. Below the Curie temperature (T ), P in PTO generates a depolarization field due to opposite surface-bound charges, which destabilizes the polarization38. Effective screening or compensation of these charges is crucial for stabilizing a single-domain structure24,39. For pure PTO film, positively charged oxygen vacancies typically screen negatively charged surfaces, while electrons from the electrode compensate for positively charged surfaces, as revealed in PbZr Ti O and BFO films25,27. As a comparison, the cross-section microstructure of Ta-PTO film was systemically characterized by using advanced electron microscopy techniques to understand its screening mechanism.

Fig. 2a,d indicate an atomically sharp interface and a smooth surface of the Ta-PTO film. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) line scanning (Fig. 2b) shows a decrease in the Ti signal and an increase in the Ta signal within three unit cells near the interface, while the Pb signal remains nearly unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 7a–c). In addition, a significant enhancement of Ta signals near the interface (Fig. 2c) can be confirmed by time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS). These results support that Ta dopants probably occupy Ti sites in the perovskite tetragonal PTO lattice. The electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) characterizations indicate that Ta doping induces oxygen vacancies near the interface (Supplementary Fig. 8). The relatively higher peak 2 compared to peak 1 in the upper O-K spectra confirms that oxygen vacancies are largely confined within ~4 nm near the Ta-PTO film interface40. Meanwhile, the Pb intensity decreases towards the surface within ~5 nm of the Ta-PTO thin film (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 7d–e). Additionally, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirms the presence of Pb vacancies in the surface layer (Supplementary Fig. 9) and reveals that the Pb/Ti ratio in Ta-PTO film is ~14.1% lower than in pure PTO film. Therefore, in single-domain Ta-PTO thin films, the polarization screening by negatively charged Pb vacancies and positively charged oxygen vacancies stabilizes the upward polarization, as shown in Fig. 2f.

In addition, the Ti ion displacement related to Pb position has been used to determine the polarization intensity. For example, the P intensity of PTO is ~67 μC cm-2 when the displacement is ~0.38 Å24. In contrast, Ta-PTO shows a reduced polarization intensity with a ~0.2 Å displacement, corresponding to a Pb vacancy concentration of ~16% that can be inferred by complete polarization screening (34 μC cm-2) near the surface.

The screening mechanism in Fig. 2f could mediate a band structure of Ta-PTO films. To understand this issue, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations (Supplementary Note 2). The calculations were conducted at a 12.5% concentration of both Pb vacancies and Ta substitutions (Supplementary Fig. 10). The results revealed that Ta substitution for Ti (Ta· ) is more easily formed acting as an effective donor, while Pb vacancies behave as an acceptor. The local density of states (LDOS) across Ta-doped, pristine, and Pb-vacancy-rich regions in Fig. 2g,h indicate a type-II band alignment. In the Pb-vacancy-rich region, the Fermi level is closer to the valence band maximum (VBM), raising both the VBM and conduction band minimum (CBM) by ~0.2 eV. Conversely, in the Ta-doped region, the Fermi level is closer to the CBM, lowering both the CBM and VBM by a similar energy offset. To this end, we have illustrated the energy band structure of Ta-PTO (Fig. 2i). The synergistic effect of surface Pb vacancies, the pristine phase, and the Ta-doped interfacial layer collectively forms a band bending structure and corresponding built-in electric field that is analogy to a p-i-n structure. Moreover, the presence of a built-in electric field was further verified by kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) (Supplementary Fig. 11 and Supplementary Fig. 12)41, where the surface potential was found and decreased gradually from the Ta-PTO film surface towards the NSTO substrate.

Since a p-i-n structure is available in Ta-PTO film, it is interesting to explore PV performance of Ta-PTO film (~2.8 eV in bandgap) using a 375 nm linearly polarized laser. Fig. 3a,b show the current density-voltage (J-V) characteristics of the films under light excitation and dark field, respectively. Under zero bias, Ta-PTO film achieves an ultrahigh short-circuit current (J ) of 1018.5 μA (~130 mA cm-2), remarkably surpassing the 31.6 μA (~4.03 mA cm- 2) observed in pure PTO film under 500 mW cm-2 irradiation. The corresponding open-circuit voltage (V ) is ~1.31 V, exceeding the ~1.22 V of pure PTO film. Notably, the pure PTO film exhibits a linear J-V curve in the -1.5 to 1.5 V voltage range, indicating typical bulk PV behavior42. In contrast, Ta-PTO film shows a nonlinear J-V response, which is probably attributed to a p-i-n structure, as shown in Fig. 2i.

To further evaluate the PV performance of the Ta-PTO film, the response under varying light intensities (I ) were measured. J increases almost linearly with I due to the generation of more photogenerated carriers. In contrast, V gradually saturates as the quasi-Fermi level separation reaches its limit (Fig. 3c)4. As shown in Fig. 3d, the J response to the on-off switching of light at zero bias demonstrated excellent control and stability. To accurately assess the response speed of the Ta-PTO film, a time-resolved pulse response system was utilized with a 266 nm pulsed laser. The zero bias pulse response, shown in Fig. 3e, reveals a rise time (t) of ~0.49 μs (10% to 90%) and a decay time (t ) of ~15.66 μs (90% to 10%). Fig. 3f shows the photoresponsivity (R = J /I ) under zero bias and different wavelengths, with a maximum value reaching 0.5078 A W-1 at 375 nm (I = 50 mW cm-2) and 0.1477 A W-1 at 254 nm (I = 4.09 mW cm-2) (Supplementary Fig. 13). Moreover, R of Ta-PTO film was compared with different UV detectors based on ferroelectric and classic semiconductors from literatures, as presented in Fig. 3g. Remarkably, its self-powered response surpasses emerging ferroelectric materials by over two orders of magnitude. In the deep ultraviolet region, the responsivity of the Ta-PTO detector surpasses that of p-i-n structured third-generation semiconductors, such as GaN and SiC (Supplementary Table 1).

Ta-PTO film device exhibits outstanding PV performance not only in the UV range but also in the hard X-ray band (10–100 keV). For long-term device applications, the structural stability of perovskite ferroelectric oxides is highly desirable compared to halide perovskite43. More attractively, its high density (~7.52 g cm-3) and the large atomic number for Pb (82), makes the film attractive for direct-type X-ray detector. To evaluate the photon absorption properties, the photon cross-section database44 was used in conjunction with the material densities to calculate the photon absorption spectra of Si, amorphous Se, CdZnTe (CZT), organic-inorganic hybrid halide perovskite methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbBr ; MA = CH NH +), purely inorganic halide perovskite CsPbBr , and PTO in the X-ray energy range of 0.001 to 1 MeV (Fig. 4a). Due to its high theoretical density, and disregarding K, L, and M edge resonant absorptions, PTO demonstrates an obvious advantage in absorption coefficient across the entire photon energy range.

The J-V characteristics of the Ta-PTO film detector under X-ray irradiation and in dark conditions are shown in Fig. 4b. A key performance for X-ray detectors is sensitivity (C Gy – 1 air cm–3), which is calculated by determining the slope of the linear region in the current density-dose rate relationship and multiplying it by the active layer thickness. The Ta-PTO film detector achieved an impressive sensitivity of 4.73 C Gy –1 cm–3 (Fig. 4c). As compared in Supplementary Table 2, the sensitivity of Ta-PTO detector under zero bias is much higher than those of typical X-ray detection materials. It is approximately three orders of magnitude higher than that of commercial amorphous Se detectors (0.00125 C Gy –1 cm–3) operating under a 2 kV bias, and about 50 times higher than that of CZT detectors (0.087 C Gy –1 cm–3). Furthermore, it surpasses the performance of CsPbBr₃ thin films (0.26 C Gy –1 cm–3) and two-dimensional layered perovskite (BA) (MA) Pb I (0.276 C Gy –1 cm–3) under zero bias, indicating its superior sensitivity for advanced X-ray detection.

An ultra-low dark current of 1.8 nA cm-2 has been obtained in the detector at zero bias, resulting in an on/off ratio exceeding 500 and stable switching behavior (Supplementary Fig. 14). The radiation tolerance of the detector was evaluated by subjecting it to X-ray radiation at a dose rate of 1.46 mGy s-1 for a total duration of 2.5 h, where a cumulative dose is up to 14 Gyₐᵢᵣ, approximately equivalent to the dose received from 10,000 chest digital radiography (DR) scans45. These performances confirm the excellent radiation stability of the Ta-PTO detector, highlighting its reliability under extended exposure to X-ray irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 15). As shown in Fig. 4d, we further constructed an automated scanning system to evaluate the self-powered X-ray imaging capability of the detector. A seahorse specimen and coil spring were selected as the imaging target (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 16a,b), successfully visualizing both the external outline and internal structure of the samples under zero bias (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 16c). In contrast, a commercial amorphous Se detector failed to obtain similar imaging resolution by using the same seahorse specimen (Supplementary Fig. 17).

In summary, we report a polarization-controlled PV response in single-domain PTO films by interfacial Ta dopant. An ultrahigh PV current of ~130 mA cm-2 at 375 nm was obtained and the corresponding photoresponsivity under zero bias was 100 times higher than those of the emerged ferroelectrics. Interestingly, a self-powered X-ray detector with excellent sensitivity has been fabricated using this film, enabling high-quality specimen imaging under X-ray exposure. Theoretical and experimental studies reveal that interfacial Ta doping during solution epitaxy controls the polarization direction via flexoelectric effect, while simultaneously creating a Pb vacancy layer near the film surface for polarization screening. Both n-type interfacial doping and p-type surface defect layers generate a p-i-n structure throughout the film, leading to the observed photovoltaic properties and enhanced device performance. Our findings could pave a new way for energy conversion and optoelectronic devices ranging from UV to X-ray band by using ferroelectric materials.
paper_content.methods:
Materials.
Lead nitrate (Pb(NO ) , ≥99.999%), tetrabutyl titanate (TBOT, ≥98%) were purchased from Aladdin Chemistry Co. Tantalum pentoxide (Ta O , ≥99.999%) was purchased from Alfa Aesar. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, ≥85.0%), acetone (≥99.5%) and ethanol (≥99.7%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. All the reagents were used as received. single-crystal 0.7 wt.% Nb doped SrTiO (NSTO) substrates with dimensions 10 × 10 × 0.5 mm3 and (100) orientation were obtained from Shanghai Institute of Optics and Mechanics.

Film preparation.
As shown in the Supplementary Fig. 18, PTO and Ta-PTO thin films were synthesized by a hydrothermal solution-epitaxy method. Pb(NO ) , TBOT and Ta O were used as metal precursors, and KOH served as the mineralizer. NSTO single-crystal substrates were ultrasonically cleaned in acetone, ethanol, deionized water, and ethanol sequentially, and then placed in a Teflon holder for drying.

In a Teflon liner, 15 mL of deionized water was first added. KOH (9.54 g) was dissolved to prepare a solution with a total precursor concentration of 6.8 M. Subsequently, 1.708 mL of TBOT was added under vigorous stirring. For Ta-PTO growth, Ta O was introduced at 0.11 g, corresponding to a Ta substitution level of 10 mol% (Ta/(Ta+Ti) = 10%). The Pb/Ti molar ratio was maintained at 1.25:1 to compensate for Pb volatility. Accordingly, Pb(NO ) (2.04 g) was dissolved separately in 10 mL of deionized water and then added dropwise into the precursor solution under continuous stirring.

After stirring for 2 h at room temperature, the NSTO substrate was placed horizontally in the precursor solution, positioned approximately 15 mm above the bottom of the Teflon liner. The Teflon liner was then sealed inside a stainless-steel autoclave, and the hydrothermal epitaxial growth was carried out at 200 °C for 12 h. After the reaction, the samples were thoroughly cleaned by repeated ultrasonication in deionized water and ethanol, and then dried in air at 60 °C.

Characterization.
The structures of the sample were characterized by Scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi SU-70 Analytical FESEM), X-ray Diffraction (XRD, Thermo ARL X’TRA powder diffractometer, Cu Kα radiation, λ=1.54056 Å), Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM, Asylum Research, Cypher S and MFP-3D), X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi). An integrated Focused Ion Beam (FIB, Helios nanolab 600) and SEM (Hatachi S4700) was used to extract thin-film lamellae from the bulk sample, Pt and Au layers were deposited on film surface to protect from damage and increase the conductivity, respectively. Subsequent cross-sectional observations of the film were carried out using aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope (FEI Titan G2 80-200 Chemi STEM, ThermoFisher Spectra 300). The variation in composition across the thickness of PTO films were characterized by Time-of-flight secondary-ion mass (TOTF-SIMS, IONTOF GmbH TOF.SIMS 5-100).

Ti-ion displacement analysis.
Ti off-center displacements were quantified from atomic-level HAADF-STEM images by measuring the offset between each Ti atomic column and the geometric center of its four nearest Pb neighbors. Atomic column positions were determined using Gaussian peak fitting, and the out-of-plane displacement component was extracted to evaluate local polarization. Displacement statistics were collected over multiple unit cells to analyze polarization variation across the film thickness.

Photovoltaic measurement.
Photovoltaic properties of PTO and Ta-PTO films were collected using optical units from Thorlabs and source measure units (Keithley 2450). Top Ag electrodes (diameter: ~1 mm, thickness: ~20 nm, determined using an ellipsometer) were deposited by magnetron sputtering (VCT300) on the PTO surface as the top electrode and NSTO substrate acted as the bottom electrode. The films were illuminated with light sources including a 254 nm UV mercury lamp (XingChuangUV) and lasers at 266 nm (MPL-F-266), 375 nm (MDL-III-375), 405 nm (MDL-III-405), and 532 nm (MGL-III-532). The response time was measured using a preamplifier (Stanford Research Systems SR570) in conjunction with an oscilloscope (Tektronix TBS2204B).

X-ray detection performance measurement.
The X-ray detection performance evaluation was carried out by using an Amptek Mini-X2 tube with the energy of ≤50 keV and peak intensity at 22 keV. The output cone angle of X-ray was 120°, and the tube voltage was kept at 50 kV. A Radcal Accu-Gold+10X6-180 ion chamber dosimeter was used to calibrate the dose rate, which was adjusted by varying the tube current. The X-ray detector was placed at the same position as the dosimeter. The photocurrent and dark current from the device were recorded using a source measure units (Keithley 2635B).

For the X-ray imaging test, a single-pixel imaging system was constructed. A lead mask with a 0.5×0.5 mm² hole was used to collimate the incident X-rays. The object to be imaged was moved between the X-ray source and the detector using an X-Y linear stage (PI M-406.2DG) with a step size of 300 µm. The photocurrent at each point was recorded using a source measure units (Keithley 2635B). For comparison, the remote-vision mobile DR uDR 380i Pro amorphous Se imaging device from Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare was used.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors investigate single-crystal Ta-doped PbTiO3 films grown by solution epitaxy for the purpose of energy
conversion and optoelectronic applications. They first characterize the structural and ferroelectric properties of the Ta-PTO
films using a variety of complementary techniques, such as transmission electron microscopy, scanning probe microscopy
and X-ray based techniques and compare them with pristine PTO films of the same thickness. This allows them to
understand the screening mechanisms which lead to the formation of a single-domain state in Ta-PTO.
Beyond this characterization, the authors continue by investigating the photo voltaic performance of their Ta-PTO film, and
compare their results with other ferroelectric systems, as well as commercially available products. It is revealed, that Ta-PTO
performs significantly better (by approx. 2 orders of magnitude) than other ferroelectric systems that have been investigated
in literature so far. Finally, the authors developed a proof-of-concept self-powered X-ray detector, using the Ta-PTO films,
and demonstrate its performance under various conditions and compare them with the current state-of-the-art detectors.
The manuscript is well-written, rigorous and their conclusions are well-supported by their findings. I recommend the
manuscript for publication in Nature Communications after some minor revisions and answers to some remaining questions:
1. Can the authors provide an estimate on how high the Ta-doping of the PTO films is and include it when introducing them?
2. In figures 1 a,b the authors show the displacement of the Ti ion with respect to the Pb ions. Could the authors provide a
couple of sentences in the methods section on how these displacements were obtained from the HAADF-STEM images.
3. In figure 1 e,f the authors show GPA-based strain maps. Could the authors include where the 0-strain reference for these
maps was chosen (I assume in the substrate).
4. Also in figure 1 e, from the position of the arrow indicating the interface with the substrate in this map, it appears that the
compressive strain is primarily located in the substrate, while the EDS lineprofiles provided in Figures 2b and S6 show the
tantalum is incorporated in the first layers of the PTO film. Is the interface marked incorrectly in the strain map, or does
the incorporation of Ta really compressively strain the STO substrate?
5. The authors mention, that the substitution of Ti4+ with Ta5+ induces the formation of oxygen vacancies. Do they have an
explanation for the mechanism that leads to this or provide a reference that explains it?
6. The presence of oxygen vacancies at the substrate interface is supported by EELS-data of the O-K edge in Fig. S7. Could
the authors provide the ratio of intnsity between peaks 1/2 to highlight the changes in the O-K edge with distance to the
interface, as they are a bit difficult to make out from the line-plot alone.
7. In lines 194-195 the authors state "polarization screening from downward to upward switching can be realized...". I believe
what they meant to say is "charge screening of the upward facing polarization can be realized/is realized by", as they do not
perform polarization switching experiments to my understanding.
8. In order to PV performance of the PTO films, the authors have to cap their films with a metal (here Ag) electrode. Have the
authors considered that the introduction of this additional metal-interface could influence the polarization state of the
ferroelectric below? How would this interface influence the presence/formation of lead vacancies at the surface?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The present manuscript titled “Solution epitaxy of single crystal ferroelectric p-i-n structure with ultra high photovoltaic
response” is about demonstrating the high short-circuit current, which is two orders of magnitude larger than the value
reported in the literature pertaining to ferroelectric photovoltaic effect. Although the films fabricated by solution epitaxy show
better photovoltaic results, the manuscript has serious flaws in terms of the film geometry proposed for the PV studies, the
claimed ferroelectric photovoltaic effect and the mechanism proposed. The following are the detailed comments.
1. The fabrication method given in the supplementary section is not very clear. What do they mean by single-crystal
ferroelectric film? Is it epitaxy? If so, further measurements like reciprocal space mapping have to be given.
2. If I understood correctly, they have doped Ta into the PbTiO3. Is it doped throughout the film or only at the interface? As
per the manuscript, I presume that the Ta is doped throughout the film. In that case, what do they mean by Ta interfacial
doping? The entire mechanism explained in this manuscript is based on the Ta at the interface. However, it is very difficult to
follow the formation of Ta doping only at the interface.
3. Again, the Pb vacancies at the top surface are not clearly brought out in this manuscript, which is also crucial to
understand the mechanism proposed in this manuscript.
4. Overall, the formation of p-i-n structure is difficult to understand based on the fabrication details given in this manuscript.
5. What is the role of ferroelectricity in the observed PV response? A lot has been discussed in the introduction related to the
ferroelectric photovoltaic effect. But the proof for ferroelectric PV is still not clear in this manuscript.
6. Proof for the ferroelectric nature of the grown film, like P-E measurement, domain switching studied by PFM, etc, which
are essential to ascertain the ferroelectric nature of the film, are missing in this manuscript.
7. In case the observed PV effect is purely based on the p-i-n effect, then the value of the short-circuit current should not be
compared to the literature value on the ferroelectric photovoltaic system.
8. If it is due to the ferroelectric PV effect, proof for the switchable PV effect should be given, which is missing in this
manuscript.
9. In addition, some of the sentences are not clear. Examples are given below
“The photovoltaic (PV) effect for semiconductors affords versatile applications from solar
Cells…..”
“Piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM) confirms a single-domain structure of Ta-PTO film with typical ferroelectric and
piezoelectric characteristics (Supplementary Fig. 1d).” Contrary to this statement, the figure does not give any details about
the piezoelectric characteristics.
“ At the nanoscale, a large stress gradient (e.g., with the force applied through an AFM tip) can induce a local electric field
through a flexoelectric effect, which is capable to switch the local polarization”. This is confusing. Where from the AFM tip
induced flexoelectric field is coming in this study? The flexoelectric field could be the compressive strain gradient at the
interface.
“The results revealed that Ta substitution for Ti (TaTi · ) is more easily formed acting as an effective donor, while Pb
vacancies behave as an acceptor.” Where is the proof?
The discussion about the Pb-vacancy-rich region and the Ta-doped region is very vague from the perspective of the grown
Ta-doped PbTiO3.
Overall, the clarity about the samples subjected to this study itself not very clear in this manuscript. Moreover, the
mechanism proposed for the observed ultra-high PV response based on the p-i-n structure is not clearly brought out in this
manuscript. Without the proof for the ferroelectric PV effect, the value of short-circuit current reported in this manuscript is
indeed comparable only to the semiconductor-based PV effect, and it should not be compared to the ferroelectric PV effect.
Due top these flaws, I am not recommending the manuscript for publication.

Response to Reviewers’ Comments
We would like to thank both reviewers for all the constructive comments and suggestions,
which significantly help us improve the quality of the present work. We made a detailed
response to the reviewers’ comments point by point. Accordingly, the manuscript has been
carefully revised by providing additional experiments and discussions. The revised parts of the
manuscript are highlighted in red.
Reviewer #1
Question 1: Can the authors provide an estimate on how high the Ta-doping of the PTO films
is and include it when introducing them?
Response: Thank you for your constructive comments. In this work, the Ta-PTO films were
prepared by using a precursor solution with a nominal Ta content of 10 mol% (Ta/(Ta+Ti) =
10%). Regarding the absolute Ta concentration in the interfacial layer, we argue that
quantitative determination by conventional EDS is rather challenging because the Ta-rich
region is a few unit cells in thickness, and the EDS analysis inevitably involves signals from
the adjacent NSTO substrate. This made an estimation of Ta/Ti ratio being difficult to quantify.
Accordingly, we employed the nominal Ta content in the precursor.

Question 2: In figures 1 a,b the authors show the displacement of the Ti ion with respect to the
Pb ions. Could the authors provide a couple of sentences in the methods section on how these
displacements were obtained from the HAADF-STEM images.
Response: Thank you for your constructive comments. In PTO, both the oxygen octahedra and
the titanium ions undergo cooperative displacements relative to the center of the lead-sublattice
tetragonal unit cell, giving rise to the spontaneous polarization. Therefore, the off-center
displacement of the Ti ions can be directly used to quantitatively determine the polarization
state of a PTO unit cell1. Fig. R1 shows a schematic of the measurement for determining the
average displacement of a Ti ion relative to the centers of its four nearest neighboring Pb ion
columns. Based on this, we experimentally extracted the Ti-ion displacements in both pure
PTO (Fig. 1a) and Ta-PTO (Fig. 1b) thin films using cross-sectional high-angle annular dark-
field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images, and quantitatively
analyzed the distribution of these displacement values as a function of distance from the
interface.
We have now added a concise description of this displacement-extraction procedure in
the Methods section to improve clarity and reproducibility.

Question 3: In figure 1 e,f the authors show GPA-based strain maps. Could the authors include
where the 0-strain reference for these maps was chosen (I assume in the substrate).
Response: Thank you for your constructive comments. In the GPA results shown in the original
manuscript, due to the default calculation mode of the data-processing software
(DigitalMicrograph), the overall average lattice of the selected area was used as the strain
reference, which led to an offset in the strain maps. To more rigorously reflect the physical
strain state, we provided the GPA data by taking the NSTO substrate as the zero-strain reference.
The corresponding results are shown in Fig. R2.
Fig. R2 | a,b, GPA-based c-axis strain mapping at the interface for (a) pure PTO and (b) Ta-PTO films.
Question 4: Also in figure 1 e, from the position of the arrow indicating the interface with the
substrate in this map, it appears that the compressive strain is primarily located in the substrate,
while the EDS lineprofiles provided in Figures 2b and S6 show the tantalum is incorporated in
the first layers of the PTO film. Is the interface marked incorrectly in the strain map, or does
the incorporation of Ta really compressively strain the STO substrate?
Response: Thank you for your constructive comments. The interface in the strain map is
marked correctly. Consistent with the EDS line profiles in Figs. 2b and S6, Ta is incorporated
within a few unit cells on the PTO side adjacent to the interface, and there is no evidence that
the STO substrate is compressively strained.
Quantitative analysis of unit cell parameters from atomic-level HAADF-STEM images
confirms that the NSTO substrate remains unstrained near the interface, and that the
compressive strain is confined to the interfacial Ta-PTO layers (Fig. 1d). The strain field
extracted by GPA is the result of Fourier filtering and averaging on a limited spatial scale.
When the substrate is used as a reference, a mask of appropriate size can better track the phase
information of the NSTO region. However, near the abrupt interface, the reduction of the c-
axis spacing in the Ta-rich PTO layer makes its lattice frequency closer to that of the substrate,
causing some PTO signals to be included in the same phase field. This amplifies the contrast
of compressive and tensile strains at the interface and shifts the apparent strain extreme
positions towards the substrate side by approximately 1–2 unit cells.
Question 5: The authors mention, that the substitution of Ti4+ with Ta5+ induces the formation
of oxygen vacancies. Do they have an explanation for the mechanism that leads to this or
provide a reference that explains it?
Response: Thank you for your constructive comments. Ta substitution does not intrinsically
induce oxygen vacancies. From a defect-thermodynamic perspective, Ta preferentially
substitutes on the Ti site as a donor, contributes extra electrons and shifts the Fermi level
upward toward the conduction band, making PTO more n-type2. Under donor-induced n-type
conditions, the formation energy of positively charged oxygen vacancies increases with the
Fermi level. Hence, this leads to a thermodynamic suppression of oxygen vacancy formation,
which has been verified experimentally in Ta-doped PTO with a reduced oxygen-vacancy
concentration3.
However, First-principles studies have investigated that oxygen-vacancy formation energies
are sensitive to an applied strain, with both the sign and magnitude of the effect governed by
the vacancy formation volume and elastic coupling4. In our case, the Ta-induced interfacial
lattice strain gradient is proposed to drive local oxygen-vacancy formation near the interface.
Additionally, the substitution of Ti4+ by Ta5+ in PTO must satisfy charge neutrality. Atomic-
level HAADF-STEM analysis near the interface (Fig. R3) shows a clear reduction of the Ti-
column intensity within several unit cells. This suggests that the positive charges introduced
by Ta substitution and oxygen vacancies are mainly compensated by negatively charged Ti
vacancies in the interfacial region. This observation is consistent with first-principles
calculations for PTO, which show that under n-type (high-E ) conditions Ti vacancies are much
F
more stable than Pb vacancies5.

Question 7: In lines 194-195 the authors state "polarization screening from downward to
upward switching can be realized...". I believe what they meant to say is "charge screening of
the upward facing polarization can be realized/is realized by", as they do not perform
polarization switching experiments to my understanding.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and agree that the sentence in the
original manuscript could be misleading. We attempted to explain that compared with pure
PTO the Ta-doped structure creates a different charge-screening environment that stabilizes the
upward polarization state (the reversed polarization orientation) due to interfacial oxygen
vacancy and surface Pb vacancy. Therefore, we have revised the text by replacing
“polarization screening from downward to upward switching” with “charge screening
that stabilizes the upward polarization”, and we have removed the word “switching” to
avoid confusion.

Therefore, in single-domain Ta-PTO thin films, polarization screening from downward to
upward switching can be realized by negatively charged Pb vacancies and positively charged
oxygen vacancies the polarization screening by negatively charged Pb vacancies and positively

Question 8: In order to PV performance of the PTO films, the authors have to cap their films
with a metal (here Ag) electrode. Have the authors considered that the introduction of this
additional metal-interface could influence the polarization state of the ferroelectric below?
How would this interface influence the presence/formation of lead vacancies at the surface?
Response: Thank you for your constructive comments. We clarify that the polarization state in
Ta-PTO films is not affected by the metal electrode.
First, the polarization orientation is confirmed before metal deposition by PFM on the free
surface. As shown in Fig. R5a–c, the written regions show distinct phase contrast consistent
with polarization reversal (Fig. R5c) after applying programmed bias patterns (Fig. R5b).
Notably, the region poled with a negative bias at the center showed the same phase state as the
unpoled background, indicating that the as-prepared Ta-PTO film is initially in a single-domain
state with an upward polarization. The focused ion beam (FIB) sample was protected by an
Ag/W multilayer before processing, HAADF-STEM reveals downward Ti off-centering
direction (Fig. R5d), demonstrating that the polarization direction remains upward below the
metal cap region. This provides direct evidence that the polarization state is not affected by the
additional metal interface.
Second, surface sensitive XPS shows that a Pb vacancy rich surface already exists in the as-
grown Ta-PTO film (Supplementary Fig. 9). In addition, we performed atomic-level HAADF-
STEM analysis on samples prepared with a protective metal capping layer and compared Ta-
PTO with pure PTO (Fig. R6). A clear reduction of the Pb column intensity is observed near
the Ta-PTO surface, whereas the pure PTO sample remains nearly unchanged. This indicates
that the Pb vacancies at surface is an intrinsic feature of Ta-PTO formed during growth, and
will not be affected by additional metal-interface.
Third, it is unlikely that metal deposition introduces additional Pb vacancies. Pb vacancies
exhibit a much higher formation energy (~6.1 eV) than that of oxygen vacancies (~2.9 eV), and
are therefore not expected to form during conventional Ag sputtering or evaporation6.
Consistently, sputtering processes in oxides are well known to favor oxygen vacancy formation
over A-site cation loss7.

Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out that the fabrication description in the

a single-crystalline epitaxial film grown on a single-crystal substrate. Specifically, the film
displays a clearly defined in-plane epitaxial registry with the substrate. As suggested, we have
added a reciprocal space mapping (RSM) analysis. The RSM around the asymmetric (103)
reflection (Fig. R8a) shows a single Ta-PTO (103) diffraction peak together with the NSTO

narrow full width at half maximum (FWHM), indicating the high crystalline quality of the Ta-

In the revised manuscript, the main text has been updated to include the RSM analysis,
and the corresponding supplementary figures have been renumbered accordingly. This

mechanism explained in this manuscript is based on the Ta at the interface. However, it is very

Response: Thank you for your constructive comments. We clarify that the doping occurred at
the interface rather than homogeneous bulk doping of the PTO film based on our experimental
results. Firstly, the cross-sectional STEM-EDS line scan (Fig. R9b) reveals a clear Ta signal
confined to the interfacial region, with Ta intensity close to the background level away from
the interface. Second, the TOF-SIMS depth profile (Fig. R9c) shows a sharp Ta peak precisely
at the interface, while the Ta signal remains close to the detection limit throughout the bulk of
the PTO film. Therefore, by “Ta interfacial doping,” we specifically refer to the formation of a
Ta-rich interfacial layer with a thickness of only a few unit cells, instead of Ta doping
throughout PTO film.
Fig. R9 | Atomic-scale evidence for interfacial Ta doping in Ta-PTO film. a, Atomic-level cross-sectional
HAADF-STEM image of the Ta-PTO/NSTO interface. b, Elemental linear scanning profiles of Ti and Ta
element throughout Ta-PTO/NSTO interface. c, TOF-SIMS for the depth profiling of Ta-PTO film.
Based on Fig. R10, we attribute the interfacial Ta incorporation to a kinetically driven
competitive growth process during solution epitaxy. In the early stage (≈6 h), the solution is
still Ta-rich and the film is in its initial nucleation stage, so Ta can be easily incorporated into
the bottom layers that form first, creating a Ta-rich interfacial region. As the reaction progresses,
large numbers of Ta-rich particulate phases appear. These particles effectively consume the
available Ta species in the solution. EDS statistics show that the Ta fraction in the Ta-rich
particles increases sharply with reaction time. When a reaction time is above 6h, the Ta species
are consumed by the particulate phase, which strongly limits their availability for further
incorporation into the growing film10,11. As a result, the film naturally forms a Ta-rich
interfacial region, rather than Ta doping throughout PTO film.

Question 3: Again, the Pb vacancies at the top surface are not clearly brought out in this
manuscript, which is also crucial to understand the mechanism proposed in this manuscript.
Response: Thank you for your constructive comments. In our low-temperature solution epitaxy,
the Ta-PTO film has a single-domain state with upward polarization, which creates a positively
polarized top surface. Such a surface should be compensated by negative charges to stabilize
the single-domain configuration. These negative charges can be effectively provided by surface
Pb vacancies, which serve as an efficient screening mechanism for polarization-bound charges.
This screening reduces the electrostatic energy of the polarized surface and is therefore
thermodynamically favorable for stabilizing the single-domain configuration, as previously
reported for ferroelectric films12.
The existing Pb vacancies have been well established by the following solid evidences. Our
HAADF-STEM analysis shows a clear reduction of the Pb signal near the top surface (Fig.
R11b). Consistently, the Pb atomic columns intensity decreases markedly toward the surface,
whereas the Ti-column intensity remains comparatively stable (Fig. R11d,e). In addition,
surface-sensitive XPS further supports Pb deficiency at the film surface, the measured Pb/Ti
ratio is lower for Ta-PTO than for pure PTO (Supplementary Fig. 9), consistent with the
presence of a Pb vacancies.

sectional HAADF-STEM image of the Ta-PTO surface region. b, Elemental linear scanning profiles of Ti

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Ferroelectric materials with a switchable polarization are appealing for optoelectronic applications because of their above-bandgap photovoltage with a potential to exceed the Shockley-Queisser limit efficiency within classic p-n junctions. However, the intrinsic photovoltaic current in ferroelectrics remains far below the junction ones by orders, hindering their practical applications. Here we report an extremely large photovoltaic current density of 130 mA cm-2 with a photovoltage of 1.31 V under 375 nm light illumination in single-domain lead titanate films. Its photoresponsivity surpasses all available ferroelectric materials by two orders of magnitude. Systematic investigations reveal that an interfacial Ta dopant layer during solution epitaxy drives a polarization converting of the film via the flexoelectric effect, where surface charged Pb vacancy layer was generated for polarization screening. These two layers produce a p-i-n structure throughout the film, accounting for the ultrahigh photovoltaic response. Furthermore, a self-powered X-ray detector made of such film was explored to achieve a sensitivity of 4.73 C Gy –1 air cm–3, three orders of magnitude higher than that of commercial amorphous Se detectors. Our findings may pave the way for exploring novel detection and imaging devices based on ferroelectric materials.

---

## Introduction

The photovoltaic (PV) effect in semiconductors is the foundation of many technologies, such as solar energy conversion1, photocatalysis2 and optoelectronic sensing3. The key step to these applications is efficiently driving charge separation of electron-hole pair carriers or excitons by a built-in electric field and subsequent carrier transport. Towards this purpose, classic p-n junction was fabricated in the crystalline silicon solar cells. Nevertheless, the efficiency of solar-cell is curtailed by inherent energy losses, subjected to the Shockley-Queisser (S-Q) limit in single p-n junction4,5. Alternatively, perovskite oxide ferroelectric semiconductors, have triggered great interests for solar energy conversion6–8, where the above-bandgap voltage from several to several thousand volts can even be produced in single-phase ferroelectrics such as LiNbO 9, holding a potential to exceed such efficiency limit5. Interestingly, an electric polarization-direction-dependent PV effect has been demonstrated in BiFeO 3 (BFO)10. However, the resulting PV current density turns out to be quite low mainly due to poor bulk conductivity. Different strategies ranging from the enhanced absorption by doping11, high-efficient carrier collection by atomic force microscope (AFM) tips12,13 and polar order engineering14 have been developed to improve the PV current. Despite great efforts towards polarization-based PV effect in the past decades, the intrinsic PV current in ferroelectrics is still at the level of μA cm-2. The PV current mechanisms in ferroelectrics are still complex and controversial, involving shift current, ballistic current, and incompletely screened depolarization field or domain walls15. Despite of great efforts, an effective strategy to significantly improve PV current in ferroelectrics towards practical devices remain a big challenge16.

For typical crystalline silicon or halide perovskite solar cells, the p-n junction or p-i-n structure plays a decisive role in achieving efficient energy conversion17,18, where electron and hole transport layers as well as built-in electric field design are achieved simultaneously. For example, in halide perovskite solar cells, meticulous selection of transport layers and precise band structure matching are essential for optimizing p-i-n functionality. Nevertheless, analogous transport layers and their derived built-in electric field throughout single-phase ferroelectrics have not been explored yet. But it is very encouraging that intriguing electrical conductivity phenomena near domain walls have been discovered19 and illustrated systematically20. N-type or p-type conducting layer near domain walls in ferroelectrics could be generated through spatial confinement of charged defects, such as Bi vacancies and oxygen vacancies, compensating bound charges due to a spontaneous polarization discontinuity21. Interestingly, p-n junction based on single domain wall have been designed experimentally22. These advances suggest a possibility to enhance the PV current through domain wall confining charged defects. However, non-uniform direction of built-in electric field near every domain wall is not beneficial for unidirectional photogenerated carrier separation and transport. Moreover, domain walls have been identified to contribute to the high photovoltage rather than the PV current23.

In addition to domain walls, the polarization surface of single-domain ferroelectrics have been demonstrated to energetically confine various charged point defects for screening bound charges24. In principle, these defect layers near the opposite polarization surface can serve as electron and hole transport layers, as well as constructing a p-i-n structure to enhance the PV effect. Especially, it has been proved that oxygen vacancy layer is prevailed as a screening manner near the negative polarization surface of ferroelectrics25–27. However, oxygen vacancies hardly contribute to n-type conduction in perovskite ferroelectric oxides because of forming polarons by trapping electrons28,29.

In this work, we developed a strategy to control the polarization direction of single-domain ferroelectric lead titanate (PbTiO , PTO) films by an interfacial Ta dopant during a solution epitaxy. This enables constructing a p-i-n structure throughout the films, where the interfacial Ta doping layer and the polarization screening induced surface Pb vacancy layer can be employed as efficient n-type electron and p-type hole transport layers, respectively. As a result, an ultrahigh PV current density of 130 mA cm-2 with a photovoltage of 1.31 V under 375 nm light illumination was obtained, two orders of magnitude higher than that of emerging ferroelectric materials. Using these films, a self-powered and direct-type X-ray detector was fabricated to demonstrate high sensitivity and stability which is highly desired for next generation X-ray imaging devices.

---

## Results

Single-crystal single-domain pure PTO and Ta doped PTO (Ta-PTO) films have been grown with a solution epitaxy method30 on single-crystal 0.7% Nb doped SrTiO (NSTO) substrates at a relatively low temperature (~200°C) (see methods for more details). X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed that both films exhibit a tetragonal perovskite structure (JCPDS#70-0746) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). As shown in Supplementary Fig. 1b, a single Ta-PTO (103) diffraction peak is observed together with the NSTO (103) substrate peak, indicating epitaxial growth of the Ta-PTO film on the NSTO substrate. Additionally, 𝜙 scan revealed four peaks at 90° intervals, indicating the single-crystal nature of the Ta-PTO film (Supplementary Fig. 1c), which also has a smooth and continuous surface (Supplementary Fig. 1d). For tetragonal perovskite PTO, the spontaneous polarization (P ) arises from the off-center displacements of Ti ions31, was analyzed using atomic-resolution high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Fig. 3). As shown in Fig. 1a, Ti ions in the pure PTO film display upward displacements relative to the Pb ion columns, indicating a downward polarization along the film's thickness direction. The thickness of the pure PTO film is ~1030 nm. In contrast, Fig. 1b reveals opposite displacements of Ti ions in the Ta-PTO film, with a thickness of ~1100 nm. The out-of-plane displacement of Ti ions in Ta-PTO increases to ~0.20 Å at the surface, slightly smaller than the ~0.26 Å observed for pure PTO. Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) confirms that the Ta-PTO film exhibits typical ferroelectric characteristics with a single-domain configuration (Supplementary Fig. 4). Furthermore, the rocking curves scanned around the (002) diffraction peak further confirms the single-crystal nature of the films (Supplementary Fig. 5), with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 0.385° for Ta-PTO and 0.237° for pure PTO, further supporting the single-domain configuration.

To uncover the mechanism behind the opposite polarization direction in pure PTO and Ta-PTO films, we analyzed their interface structures. Fig. 1c,d show the lattice parameters a and c. The interfacial c-value in Ta-PTO (~3.99 Å) is smaller than in pure PTO (~4.11 Å). Notably, it increases to ~4.15 Å within the first three unit cells above the interface, indicating an inhomogeneous compressive strain (~3.86%) between the interface and the inner regions of the Ta-PTO film. The interfacial strain was further analyzed using geometric phase analysis (GPA) based on atomic-level HAADF-STEM images (Supplementary Fig. 6). As shown in Fig. 1e,f, unlike pure PTO film, Ta-PTO film exhibits a distinct interfacial compressive strain (ε ) layer, likely caused by the incorporation of Ta dopants, considering the slightly larger ionic radius of Ta5+ (0.640 Å) compared to Ti4+ (0.605 Å)32. At the nanoscale, a large stress gradient can induce a local electric field via the flexoelectric effect. Such gradients can be generated artificially, for example by localized mechanical loading with an AFM tip, as widely reported to induce flexoelectric fields and control ferroelectric polarization33,34. This effect arises from the coupling between a strain gradient and ferroelectric polarization35. Moreover, phase-field modeling was used to calculate the flexoelectric field within the PTO layer caused by strain gradient from local concentration inhomogeneity36 (Supplementary Note 1). As shown in Fig. 1g, the calculated field strength at six unit cells can be up to 130 kV cm-1, much higher than the coercive field (E ) of PTO37, enabling polarization reversal. This flexoelectric effect energetically favors the reversal of the polarization direction of the Ta-PTO film layer near the interface from downward to upward, creating a built-in field that could switch the polarization throughout the film (Fig. 1h).

The opposite polarization direction of the films shown in Fig. 1a,b necessitate different screening mechanisms. Below the Curie temperature (T ), P in PTO generates a depolarization field due to opposite surface-bound charges, which destabilizes the polarization38. Effective screening or compensation of these charges is crucial for stabilizing a single-domain structure24,39. For pure PTO film, positively charged oxygen vacancies typically screen negatively charged surfaces, while electrons from the electrode compensate for positively charged surfaces, as revealed in PbZr Ti O and BFO films25,27. As a comparison, the cross-section microstructure of Ta-PTO film was systemically characterized by using advanced electron microscopy techniques to understand its screening mechanism.

Fig. 2a,d indicate an atomically sharp interface and a smooth surface of the Ta-PTO film. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) line scanning (Fig. 2b) shows a decrease in the Ti signal and an increase in the Ta signal within three unit cells near the interface, while the Pb signal remains nearly unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 7a–c). In addition, a significant enhancement of Ta signals near the interface (Fig. 2c) can be confirmed by time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS). These results support that Ta dopants probably occupy Ti sites in the perovskite tetragonal PTO lattice. The electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) characterizations indicate that Ta doping induces oxygen vacancies near the interface (Supplementary Fig. 8). The relatively higher peak 2 compared to peak 1 in the upper O-K spectra confirms that oxygen vacancies are largely confined within ~4 nm near the Ta-PTO film interface40. Meanwhile, the Pb intensity decreases towards the surface within ~5 nm of the Ta-PTO thin film (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 7d–e). Additionally, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirms the presence of Pb vacancies in the surface layer (Supplementary Fig. 9) and reveals that the Pb/Ti ratio in Ta-PTO film is ~14.1% lower than in pure PTO film. Therefore, in single-domain Ta-PTO thin films, the polarization screening by negatively charged Pb vacancies and positively charged oxygen vacancies stabilizes the upward polarization, as shown in Fig. 2f.

In addition, the Ti ion displacement related to Pb position has been used to determine the polarization intensity. For example, the P intensity of PTO is ~67 μC cm-2 when the displacement is ~0.38 Å24. In contrast, Ta-PTO shows a reduced polarization intensity with a ~0.2 Å displacement, corresponding to a Pb vacancy concentration of ~16% that can be inferred by complete polarization screening (34 μC cm-2) near the surface.

The screening mechanism in Fig. 2f could mediate a band structure of Ta-PTO films. To understand this issue, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations (Supplementary Note 2). The calculations were conducted at a 12.5% concentration of both Pb vacancies and Ta substitutions (Supplementary Fig. 10). The results revealed that Ta substitution for Ti (Ta· ) is more easily formed acting as an effective donor, while Pb vacancies behave as an acceptor. The local density of states (LDOS) across Ta-doped, pristine, and Pb-vacancy-rich regions in Fig. 2g,h indicate a type-II band alignment. In the Pb-vacancy-rich region, the Fermi level is closer to the valence band maximum (VBM), raising both the VBM and conduction band minimum (CBM) by ~0.2 eV. Conversely, in the Ta-doped region, the Fermi level is closer to the CBM, lowering both the CBM and VBM by a similar energy offset. To this end, we have illustrated the energy band structure of Ta-PTO (Fig. 2i). The synergistic effect of surface Pb vacancies, the pristine phase, and the Ta-doped interfacial layer collectively forms a band bending structure and corresponding built-in electric field that is analogy to a p-i-n structure. Moreover, the presence of a built-in electric field was further verified by kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) (Supplementary Fig. 11 and Supplementary Fig. 12)41, where the surface potential was found and decreased gradually from the Ta-PTO film surface towards the NSTO substrate.

Since a p-i-n structure is available in Ta-PTO film, it is interesting to explore PV performance of Ta-PTO film (~2.8 eV in bandgap) using a 375 nm linearly polarized laser. Fig. 3a,b show the current density-voltage (J-V) characteristics of the films under light excitation and dark field, respectively. Under zero bias, Ta-PTO film achieves an ultrahigh short-circuit current (J ) of 1018.5 μA (~130 mA cm-2), remarkably surpassing the 31.6 μA (~4.03 mA cm- 2) observed in pure PTO film under 500 mW cm-2 irradiation. The corresponding open-circuit voltage (V ) is ~1.31 V, exceeding the ~1.22 V of pure PTO film. Notably, the pure PTO film exhibits a linear J-V curve in the -1.5 to 1.5 V voltage range, indicating typical bulk PV behavior42. In contrast, Ta-PTO film shows a nonlinear J-V response, which is probably attributed to a p-i-n structure, as shown in Fig. 2i.

To further evaluate the PV performance of the Ta-PTO film, the response under varying light intensities (I ) were measured. J increases almost linearly with I due to the generation of more photogenerated carriers. In contrast, V gradually saturates as the quasi-Fermi level separation reaches its limit (Fig. 3c)4. As shown in Fig. 3d, the J response to the on-off switching of light at zero bias demonstrated excellent control and stability. To accurately assess the response speed of the Ta-PTO film, a time-resolved pulse response system was utilized with a 266 nm pulsed laser. The zero bias pulse response, shown in Fig. 3e, reveals a rise time (t) of ~0.49 μs (10% to 90%) and a decay time (t ) of ~15.66 μs (90% to 10%). Fig. 3f shows the photoresponsivity (R = J /I ) under zero bias and different wavelengths, with a maximum value reaching 0.5078 A W-1 at 375 nm (I = 50 mW cm-2) and 0.1477 A W-1 at 254 nm (I = 4.09 mW cm-2) (Supplementary Fig. 13). Moreover, R of Ta-PTO film was compared with different UV detectors based on ferroelectric and classic semiconductors from literatures, as presented in Fig. 3g. Remarkably, its self-powered response surpasses emerging ferroelectric materials by over two orders of magnitude. In the deep ultraviolet region, the responsivity of the Ta-PTO detector surpasses that of p-i-n structured third-generation semiconductors, such as GaN and SiC (Supplementary Table 1).

Ta-PTO film device exhibits outstanding PV performance not only in the UV range but also in the hard X-ray band (10–100 keV). For long-term device applications, the structural stability of perovskite ferroelectric oxides is highly desirable compared to halide perovskite43. More attractively, its high density (~7.52 g cm-3) and the large atomic number for Pb (82), makes the film attractive for direct-type X-ray detector. To evaluate the photon absorption properties, the photon cross-section database44 was used in conjunction with the material densities to calculate the photon absorption spectra of Si, amorphous Se, CdZnTe (CZT), organic-inorganic hybrid halide perovskite methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbBr ; MA = CH NH +), purely inorganic halide perovskite CsPbBr , and PTO in the X-ray energy range of 0.001 to 1 MeV (Fig. 4a). Due to its high theoretical density, and disregarding K, L, and M edge resonant absorptions, PTO demonstrates an obvious advantage in absorption coefficient across the entire photon energy range.

The J-V characteristics of the Ta-PTO film detector under X-ray irradiation and in dark conditions are shown in Fig. 4b. A key performance for X-ray detectors is sensitivity (C Gy – 1 air cm–3), which is calculated by determining the slope of the linear region in the current density-dose rate relationship and multiplying it by the active layer thickness. The Ta-PTO film detector achieved an impressive sensitivity of 4.73 C Gy –1 cm–3 (Fig. 4c). As compared in Supplementary Table 2, the sensitivity of Ta-PTO detector under zero bias is much higher than those of typical X-ray detection materials. It is approximately three orders of magnitude higher than that of commercial amorphous Se detectors (0.00125 C Gy –1 cm–3) operating under a 2 kV bias, and about 50 times higher than that of CZT detectors (0.087 C Gy –1 cm–3). Furthermore, it surpasses the performance of CsPbBr₃ thin films (0.26 C Gy –1 cm–3) and two-dimensional layered perovskite (BA) (MA) Pb I (0.276 C Gy –1 cm–3) under zero bias, indicating its superior sensitivity for advanced X-ray detection.

An ultra-low dark current of 1.8 nA cm-2 has been obtained in the detector at zero bias, resulting in an on/off ratio exceeding 500 and stable switching behavior (Supplementary Fig. 14). The radiation tolerance of the detector was evaluated by subjecting it to X-ray radiation at a dose rate of 1.46 mGy s-1 for a total duration of 2.5 h, where a cumulative dose is up to 14 Gyₐᵢᵣ, approximately equivalent to the dose received from 10,000 chest digital radiography (DR) scans45. These performances confirm the excellent radiation stability of the Ta-PTO detector, highlighting its reliability under extended exposure to X-ray irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 15). As shown in Fig. 4d, we further constructed an automated scanning system to evaluate the self-powered X-ray imaging capability of the detector. A seahorse specimen and coil spring were selected as the imaging target (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 16a,b), successfully visualizing both the external outline and internal structure of the samples under zero bias (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 16c). In contrast, a commercial amorphous Se detector failed to obtain similar imaging resolution by using the same seahorse specimen (Supplementary Fig. 17).

In summary, we report a polarization-controlled PV response in single-domain PTO films by interfacial Ta dopant. An ultrahigh PV current of ~130 mA cm-2 at 375 nm was obtained and the corresponding photoresponsivity under zero bias was 100 times higher than those of the emerged ferroelectrics. Interestingly, a self-powered X-ray detector with excellent sensitivity has been fabricated using this film, enabling high-quality specimen imaging under X-ray exposure. Theoretical and experimental studies reveal that interfacial Ta doping during solution epitaxy controls the polarization direction via flexoelectric effect, while simultaneously creating a Pb vacancy layer near the film surface for polarization screening. Both n-type interfacial doping and p-type surface defect layers generate a p-i-n structure throughout the film, leading to the observed photovoltaic properties and enhanced device performance. Our findings could pave a new way for energy conversion and optoelectronic devices ranging from UV to X-ray band by using ferroelectric materials.

## Methods

Materials.
Lead nitrate (Pb(NO ) , ≥99.999%), tetrabutyl titanate (TBOT, ≥98%) were purchased from Aladdin Chemistry Co. Tantalum pentoxide (Ta O , ≥99.999%) was purchased from Alfa Aesar. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, ≥85.0%), acetone (≥99.5%) and ethanol (≥99.7%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. All the reagents were used as received. single-crystal 0.7 wt.% Nb doped SrTiO (NSTO) substrates with dimensions 10 × 10 × 0.5 mm3 and (100) orientation were obtained from Shanghai Institute of Optics and Mechanics.

Film preparation.
As shown in the Supplementary Fig. 18, PTO and Ta-PTO thin films were synthesized by a hydrothermal solution-epitaxy method. Pb(NO ) , TBOT and Ta O were used as metal precursors, and KOH served as the mineralizer. NSTO single-crystal substrates were ultrasonically cleaned in acetone, ethanol, deionized water, and ethanol sequentially, and then placed in a Teflon holder for drying.

In a Teflon liner, 15 mL of deionized water was first added. KOH (9.54 g) was dissolved to prepare a solution with a total precursor concentration of 6.8 M. Subsequently, 1.708 mL of TBOT was added under vigorous stirring. For Ta-PTO growth, Ta O was introduced at 0.11 g, corresponding to a Ta substitution level of 10 mol% (Ta/(Ta+Ti) = 10%). The Pb/Ti molar ratio was maintained at 1.25:1 to compensate for Pb volatility. Accordingly, Pb(NO ) (2.04 g) was dissolved separately in 10 mL of deionized water and then added dropwise into the precursor solution under continuous stirring.

After stirring for 2 h at room temperature, the NSTO substrate was placed horizontally in the precursor solution, positioned approximately 15 mm above the bottom of the Teflon liner. The Teflon liner was then sealed inside a stainless-steel autoclave, and the hydrothermal epitaxial growth was carried out at 200 °C for 12 h. After the reaction, the samples were thoroughly cleaned by repeated ultrasonication in deionized water and ethanol, and then dried in air at 60 °C.

Characterization.
The structures of the sample were characterized by Scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi SU-70 Analytical FESEM), X-ray Diffraction (XRD, Thermo ARL X’TRA powder diffractometer, Cu Kα radiation, λ=1.54056 Å), Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM, Asylum Research, Cypher S and MFP-3D), X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi). An integrated Focused Ion Beam (FIB, Helios nanolab 600) and SEM (Hatachi S4700) was used to extract thin-film lamellae from the bulk sample, Pt and Au layers were deposited on film surface to protect from damage and increase the conductivity, respectively. Subsequent cross-sectional observations of the film were carried out using aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope (FEI Titan G2 80-200 Chemi STEM, ThermoFisher Spectra 300). The variation in composition across the thickness of PTO films were characterized by Time-of-flight secondary-ion mass (TOTF-SIMS, IONTOF GmbH TOF.SIMS 5-100).

Ti-ion displacement analysis.
Ti off-center displacements were quantified from atomic-level HAADF-STEM images by measuring the offset between each Ti atomic column and the geometric center of its four nearest Pb neighbors. Atomic column positions were determined using Gaussian peak fitting, and the out-of-plane displacement component was extracted to evaluate local polarization. Displacement statistics were collected over multiple unit cells to analyze polarization variation across the film thickness.

Photovoltaic measurement.
Photovoltaic properties of PTO and Ta-PTO films were collected using optical units from Thorlabs and source measure units (Keithley 2450). Top Ag electrodes (diameter: ~1 mm, thickness: ~20 nm, determined using an ellipsometer) were deposited by magnetron sputtering (VCT300) on the PTO surface as the top electrode and NSTO substrate acted as the bottom electrode. The films were illuminated with light sources including a 254 nm UV mercury lamp (XingChuangUV) and lasers at 266 nm (MPL-F-266), 375 nm (MDL-III-375), 405 nm (MDL-III-405), and 532 nm (MGL-III-532). The response time was measured using a preamplifier (Stanford Research Systems SR570) in conjunction with an oscilloscope (Tektronix TBS2204B).

X-ray detection performance measurement.
The X-ray detection performance evaluation was carried out by using an Amptek Mini-X2 tube with the energy of ≤50 keV and peak intensity at 22 keV. The output cone angle of X-ray was 120°, and the tube voltage was kept at 50 kV. A Radcal Accu-Gold+10X6-180 ion chamber dosimeter was used to calibrate the dose rate, which was adjusted by varying the tube current. The X-ray detector was placed at the same position as the dosimeter. The photocurrent and dark current from the device were recorded using a source measure units (Keithley 2635B).

For the X-ray imaging test, a single-pixel imaging system was constructed. A lead mask with a 0.5×0.5 mm² hole was used to collimate the incident X-rays. The object to be imaged was moved between the X-ray source and the detector using an X-Y linear stage (PI M-406.2DG) with a step size of 300 µm. The photocurrent at each point was recorded using a source measure units (Keithley 2635B). For comparison, the remote-vision mobile DR uDR 380i Pro amorphous Se imaging device from Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare was used.
